or on forged travel documents.  The present scale of punishment of a maximum of five years and fine might continue for other offences under
this Act.  No minimum punishment was being proposed in respect of these offences and the quantum of punishment was proposed to be left to
the discretion of the Courts.
6.         The representatives of the Ministry of Home Affairs led by the then Home Secretary and the concerned   Special Secretary made a
presentation vis-à-vis the Foreigners (Amendment) Bill, 1998, before the Committee in its meeting held on  10 September 1998. The
concerned Special Secretary of the Ministry while making a presentation, gave an overview on the Bill which inter alia   encompassed various
aspects of the influx of foreigners  into the country.  He informed the Committee that  in the year 1997, 24,91,946   passengers     arrived   and  
24,67,092   passengers   departed   through   various  exist points of India. Of the total passengers who arrived and departed, 82.91%
passengers came and departed by air, 15.65% passengers used the land route   while 1.44% relied on the sea
route.                                                                          
6.1       The Special Secretary stated that overstay after entry on valid passport and visa; entry and stay on forged or fake passport and visa; and
illegal entry and stay without any documents i.e. infiltration, unauthorised entry and stay in restricted and protected areas were some of the
major contraventions of the Foreigners  Act, 1946.  He informed the Committee that the number of cases pertaining to the forgery of passport
and visa by foreigners, detected at entry and exit points, was 550 in 1997 as against 431 in 1996, 510 in 1995 and 421 in 1994.  These figures
excluded the cases detected in the country other than the entry and exit points.
 
4
 
6.2       Speaking on the salient features of the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Special   Secretary  stated that   Section 3 of the Act provided  for
making orders for prohibiting, regulating  and restricting the entry, stay, movement and departure   of foreigners.  Those powers of the Central
Government had been entrusted to the State Governments and the UT Administrations under articles 258 and 239, respectively, with their prior
consent. Orders were issued under the Act from time to time to deal with  (1) movement of foreigners in restricted and protected areas; (2)
foreigners coming for  mountaineering expeditions, for  making  feature films  and documentary films, etc.; (3) restrictions on the    residence  
of   foreigners in certain areas, for example,  premises of areas   belonging to foreign diplomatic   mission, consular post and trade mission; and
(4) restrictions    on    taking    up    employment     by    foreigners    in    certain       sensitive  sectors such as undertakings supplying basic
services to Government  like power, water, petroleum, etc.
6.3       Thereafter, the Special Secretary dwelt on the various categories of visas issued by Indian authorities.  He said that in all, there were 15
types of visas. Diplomatic, Official, UN Diplomat and UN Official visas were governed by the Ministry of External Affairs.  The remaining
types  were governed by the Ministry of  Home Affairs.  The visas were, in fact, issued by the Indian embassies and missions located abroad. 
The policy etc., was decided at the MEA level or at the MHA level, which ever was the concerned    Ministry.   He further said that Section 14
of the Act, as it stood at present, provided for only maximum punishment up to five years imprisonment and fine for contravention of any
provision of the Act  or orders or directions  issued thereunder.  There was no provision   today for minimum punishment as also there was  no
classification of offences.
6.4       The Special Secretary, emphasising the need to amend the Foreigners Act, 1946, said that the same was a Central Act but its
implementation  was entrusted to the State  Governments and the UT Administrations.  He informed that during the Ministry’s interaction with
them, the representatives of the States and the UTs had been mentioning     about    infiltration     and    other   border-related    offences  and 
had  been recommending that keeping in view the spiral increase in the incidents of infiltration and clandestine   activities including smuggling
of arms, narcotics, etc., foreigners entry on forged  and fake travel documents, violation of  Foreigners  Act and Orders, the punishment be
made more deterrent.   The Rajasthan Government based on the experience of trans-border infiltration, smuggling of arms and ammunition,
etc., requested that the Act be made more deterrent by  providing for the offence  to be triable by the Court  of Sessions.  The intention was that
it would imply application of mind at a higher judicial level.
6.5       The Special Secretary also referred to the Fifth Report of the Estimates Committee of the 10th Lok Sabha and said that the latter while
reviewing the functioning of Consular, Passports and Visa Division of Ministry of External Affairs, had recommended that (a) punishment for
violation under Foreigners Act be made more deterrent; (b) penalties under Foreigners Act and Indian Passport Act be similar;   (c) offences be
made non-bailable with the provision for imprisonment and fine of higher deterrence, and (d) deportation on completion of sentence be made
mandatory.
6.6       The Special Secretary stated that it was in this backdrop that it was felt necessary to provide for  (a) minimum punishment; (b)
classification of punishment on the basis of gravity of contravention ; and (c) enhancement   of punishment for more serious  contraventions  
under the Act.
 
 
5
 
6.6.1    A two-fold classification of offences and punishments was proposed; (1) More stringent    punishment    in   the   form   of  
imprisonment  for  minimum   two years  and maximum eight years and with  fine  of minimum   Rs.10,000 and maximum Rs.50,000  for
serious  contraventions.   Serious contraventions would include: (i) visit to restricted/protected area without proper permit, (ii) overstay in
restricted/protected area beyond permit’s validity  in case permit    was granted, and (iii) entry, stay on forged travel documents/without
documents, and (2)  For all other contraventions of the provisions of the Act, penalty to remain same as  at  present  i.e. maximum  
imprisonment upto  five  years  and fine.  Such contraventions included:
(a)
                overstay beyond validity of visa with or without valid passport;

on tourist visa; and
(c)        punishment for abetment of any offence as mentioned in (1) and (2) above to be the same as provided in those sections for that
offence.
6.7       Enlightening the Committee on the effects of the proposed amendment, the Special Secretary said that they would be as follows:
(a)        cases mentioned in proposed Section 14A to become triable  by Sessions        Court.  This would ensure application of mind by
higher level of judicial  authority;
(b)        the Court would be required to give notice to the State  Government  thereby affording  it an opportunity   at the time   of

(c)        the recommendation made by the Estimates Committee of Parliament for making punishments under the Foreigners Act more
deterrent would stand fulfilled; and
 (d)       in the final analysis, the enhanced penalties   would make the Act more effective and deterrent in checking problems of
infiltration, overstay and other violations/contraventions of the provisions of the Foreigners Act.
7.         After the presentation of the Special Secretary, the then Home Secretary made a brief presentation before the Committee.   Underlying
the objectives behind the amendment to Section 14 of the Foreigners Act, 1946, he said that the aim was to make that Section more rigorous
than it was in its existing form.  Tracing the genesis of the Foreigners Act, he stated that the scheme of the law which was formulated a little
before Independence or on the eve of Independence  in 1946 made it clear that this law  was going to empower the executive  for prescribing, 
regulating and restricting  amongst  others the presence  and continued presence of foreigners in India. 
7.1       This law was amended six times.   Two amendments were made in 1947 and one amendment was made in 1951.  Thereafter, it was
amended in 1957 and again it was amended in 1962.  It was amended four times but six changes were made in total. 
7.2              The 1947 amendment was more substantial because of the transfer of power.
7.3       The 1951 amendment was because   of the incorporation of Hyderabad. 
7.4       It was in 1957 that the rigour of the law was slightly decreased to facilitate the free entry of nationals of Commonwealth countries. 
 
6
 
7.5       In 1962 because of relations with China the law was made more stringent.  The law was again proposed to be made more rigorous  
largely on account of the fact that situation on borders was such which called for this kind of a provision. 
7.6       He further stated that the response to the situation on borders particularly with regard   to   Pakistan   which   had     been    sending   
trained   militants    inside   India to create difficulties was  manifold. One of those difficulties was the fencing and floodlighting on Indo-Pak
border. The total length of the border with Punjab was 554 kilometers  and  almost    the entire boundary i.e. 452 kilometers  had been fenced.  
The rest could not be fenced because of geographical factors.  So far as floodlighting was concerned, 460 kilometers of area had been covered. 
One of the achievements of this fencing on the Punjab area was rapid decline in movement of militants and also there was a more effective
control on smuggling activities.   This led to the shifting of focus to other borders, namely of Rajasthan , Jammu and Kashmir and Gujarat.  In
case of Rajasthan, there was a boundary of 1,035 kms.  Of this 865 kms. had been fenced and floodlit and the work  was in progress for the
other areas.  It was felt during the last three or four years that the Rajasthan sector was very soft compared to the Punjab  sector   for
encroachment by militants.  Therefore, it was decided to study that matter in depth in consultation with the Rajasthan Government and it was
made clear by the latter that unless those operations were made triable by the Sessions Court, it would continue to be easier for the offenders to
get bail under Section 437 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
7.7       Taking up the questions from the Questionnaire prepared by the Secretariat and sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs for replies, the
Home Secretary referred to the question as to why it was Rajasthan and not other States and UTs, which came forward with the suggestion for
amendment to the Foreigners Act, 1946, he said that the matter had been engaging the attention of the  Central Government and   that in    early
1992, at a Conference of the Chief Ministers and Chief Secretaries to discuss this issue,  it was felt that a special law should be made to take
care of several of the problems that were being faced on the border.  Meanwhile, the Estimates Committee of the Parliament had also made this
recommendation in 1992 to make the provisions more stringent.   He further stated that in a different context, in November 1997, comments
were also received from the Governments of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Tripura.    Referring to the second question that had been raised
with regard to the experience of the Union Government in tackling the problem, he said that its experience had been that despite the provisions
of the Foreigners Act, it had not been possible for State Governments, Governments of the Union Territories and the Central Government   to
strictly enforce that law.  This had been on account of a variety of factors.  One of those factors was that there was a large scale influx of
infiltrators from Bangladesh, Tibet, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and a number of other places.   Another experience of the Union Government had been
that the Courts had been very lenient and that they had been granting light punishments like imprisonment for fifteen   days to one or two
months and at times only till the rising of the Court, and the fine was also largely between Rs.500 to Rs.1,000.  The experience had been that
bails too were granted.
7.8       Referring to the scheme of things obtaining  in Pakistan vis-à-vis such cases, the Home     Secretary said that Pakistan had the same
Cr.P.C.  but  when it came to the question       of   things    happening    on    their    borders, they had tightened their legal arrangement.   What
they had done was that whoever entered their country illegally would not be released on bail till the trial was over.  But it was not so in case of
India.  Therefore, the position was that in Pakistan bail was not granted at all whereas in India it was not denied.     The other point which our
law itself made clear  was   that  a  foreigner  could  not  be given  full  rights of citizenship but at the same time a

security of the country since the existing provisions of section 439 Cr.PC are not of much help in dealing with offenders under the
Foreigners Act, 1946.  Therefore, a procedure has to be formulated which is effective and at the same time reasonable and fair in law;
and in case of an alien  found  guilty under the Act, as also indulging in the acts of terrorism, the burden of proof should be on him.

with  reference to the  penal   provisions and emphasis on human rights to deal with such problems.

14.1     Clause 2 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 14 of the Foreigners Act, 1946.  This section inter alia   provides for punishment   which
may extend to five  years and fine for contravention of provisions of the Act or of any order made thereunder, or of any direction given in
pursuance of that Act or such order.  The amendment proposes to classify offences under the Foreigners Act, 1946, and to provide for
punishment depending on the gravity of offence committed.   It is also proposed that the maximum punishment under the Act may be upto
eight  years and fine upto  Rs.50,000.  As stated in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the enhancement of the punishment will
result in the serious offences  becoming  triable by Court  of  Sessions and the Court will be required to give notice to the State Government
thereby affording it an opportunity to oppose the  bail application under proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 439 of Cr.P.C, 1973.
14.2     During the examination of Clause 2 of the Bill by the Committee, the following suggestions/views were put forward:
14.2.1  It was observed that as per the proposed Section 14 any person caught with a forged passport was liable to get a punishment of
only upto five  years which was not sufficient keeping in mind the gravity of the offence. In that context, a  view was expressed that the
words “with or without valid   passport” as appearing in sub-section (b) of proposed Section 14,  should be deleted because if a person
had obtained a visa on a forged passport then it was a serious offence and hence, should not be considered a minor  infringement of the
law.
 
 
11
14.2.2  A point was raised regarding the difference in the connotation of the words “remains in India” and “stay in India” as used in
sub-sections (b) and (c) of Section 14, respectively.   It was sought to be known if there was any difference between the expressions or
they conveyed the same meaning.
14.2.3  Having noted the opinion of the Law Ministry that the proposed amendment would have the effect of making serious offences
triable by the Court of Sessions and obtaining of bail would become difficult under Section 437(3) read with Section 439(1) of  Cr.P.C.,
the Committee was not convinced with their view and was of the opinion  that there was a need to incorporate explicit provisions in the
Bill to put the matter  beyond any shadow of doubt.  In that context, it was suggested that the following may be considered for being
added at the end of proposed Section 14A:
(i)
        “Notwithstanding any provisions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the offences punishable under this Section
shall be triable by the Court of Sessions”. 
(ii) “No court shall grant bail to the accused without first affording an      opportunity to the Public Prosecutor to oppose the
bail, as provided in sub-section (1) of the Section 439, Cr.P.C., 1973”.
14.2.4  In the same context, another suggestion was put forward that a suitable provision may be incorporated in the Bill so as to
ensure that the accused persons were not able to secure bail before the trial was over.
14.2.5  Again in the same context, it was suggested that in addition to the punishment provided  in proposed Sections 14 and 14A, it
may be considered whether a ‘deportation’ clause could be added.  The idea was that the Court could, while announcing the
punishment, issue orders for deportation on completion of jail term as it was felt that such a provision could effectively tackle the
problem of large scale infiltration of foreigners into the country.
14.2.6  It was then suggested that a few Courts of Sessions should be designated as “Special Courts” for the speedy and exclusive trial
of the cases registered under the Foreigners Act, 1946.
14.2.7  A suggestion was made for laying down a specific time frame for the disposal of the cases registered under the Foreigners Act,
1946 so as to ensure that trials under the Act did not drag on indefinitely.
14.2.8  So far as ‘burden of proof’ as envisaged in Section 9 of the principal Act was concerned, it was suggested that the said Section
may be broadened and made more elaborate so as to specifically provide that the onus of burden of proof would lie, in all cases of
violation/contravention of order, rules, etc. incorporated in  Section 3 of the principal Act, on the accused persons.
14.2.9  A suggestion was made that in view of the proposed Section 14B relating to penalty for abetment  of any offence punishable
under the proposed Sections 14 and 14A, it should be examined whether any consequential amendments would be required in Section
13 of the principal Act relating to attempts, abetment, etc. to contravene the provisions of the Act. 
14.2.10  Subject to the above the  clause was adopted.

Clause 2
12.1        Clause 2 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 14 of Foreigners Act, 1946.  This section inter alia  provides for punishment which may extend to 5 years  and
fine for contravention of provisions of the Act or of any order made thereunder, or of any direction given in pursuance of that Act or such order.  The amendment
proposes to classify offences under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and to provide for punishment depending on the gravity of offence committed.   It is also proposed that
the maximum punishment under the Foreigners Act, 1946 may be upto 8 years and fine upto  Rs.50,000.  As stated in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the
Bill, the enhancement of the punishment will result in the serious offences  becoming triable by Court  of  Sessions and the Court will be required to give notice to
the State Government thereby affording it an opportunity to oppose the  bail application under proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 439 of the Cr.P.C, 1973.
12.2     During the examination of clause 2 of the Bill by the  Committee, the following suggestions/views were put forward.
 
25
 
12.2.1
    It was observed that as per the proposed Section 14 of  the Bill, any person caught with a forged passport was liable to get a
punishment of only upto 5 years which was not sufficient keeping in mind the gravity of the offence. In that context, a  view was proposed that
Section 14,  should be deleted because if a person had obtained a visa on a forged passport then it was a serious offence and hence, should not
be considered a minor  infringement of the law.
12.2.2  Another view expressed was regarding the difference in the connotation of the words “remains in India” and “stay in India” as used in
sub-sections (b) and (c) of Section 14, respectively.   It was sought to be known if there was any difference between the expressions  or they
conveyed the same meaning.
12.2.3  Having noted the opinion of the Law Ministry that the proposed amendment would have the effect of making serious offences triable
by the Court of Sessions and obtaining of bail would become difficult under Section 437(3) read with Section 439(1) of the Cr.P.C., the
Committee was not convinced with the view of the Law Ministry and  was of the opinion  that there was a need to incorporate explicit
provisions in the Bill to put the thing beyond any shadow of doubt.  In that context, it was suggested that the following may be considered for
being added at the end of proposed Section 14A:
 
(i)
                 “Notwithstanding any provisions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the offences punishable under this Section shall be triable
by the Court of Sessions”. 
(ii)                “No court shall grant bail to the accused without first affording an opportunity to the Public Prosecutor to oppose the bail, as
provided in sub-section (1) of the Section 439, Cr.P.C., 1973”.
12.2.4  In the same context, another suggestion was put forward that  a suitable provision may be incorporated in the Bill so as to ensure that
the accused persons were not able to secure bail before the trial was over.
12.2.5  Again in the same context, it was suggested that in addition to the punishment proposed in amended Sections 14 and 14A, it may be
considered whether a ‘deportation’ clause could be added.  The idea was that the Court could, while announcing the punishment, issue orders
for deportation on completion of jail term as it was felt that such a provision could effectively tackle  the problem of large scale infiltration of
foreigners into the country.
12.2.6  It was then  suggested that  a few  Courts of Sessions should be designated as “Special Courts” for the speedy and exclusive trial of the
cases registered under the Foreigners Act, 1946.
12.2.7  Another suggestion was for laying down a specific time frame for the disposal of the cases registered under the Foreigners Act, 1946 so
as to ensure that trials under the Act did not drag on indefinitely.
12.2.8  So far as ‘burden of proof’ as envisaged in Section 9 of the principal Act was concerned, it was suggested that the said Section may be
broadened and made more elaborate so as to specifically provide that the onus of burden of proof would lie, in all cases of
violation/contravention of order, rules, etc. incorporated in  Section 3 of the principal Act, on the accused persons.
12.2.9  A suggestion was made that in view of the proposed Section 14B relating to penalty for abetment   of any offence punishable under the
proposed Sections 14 and 14A, it should be examined whether any consequential amendments would be required in Section 13 of  the
principal Act relating to attempts, abetment, etc. to contravene the provisions of the Act.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
 
            Contravention of the provisions of the Foreigners Act, 1946, or of any order made thereunder, or of any direction given in pursuance  of that Act 
or such order, is punishable with imprisonment which may extend   to five  years and fine.  The cases under the Foreigners  Act are cognizable,
non-bailable  and triable by the  first class Magistrate.  However, the accused persons  arrested  under the said Act  very often manage to obtain bail under
section  437 of the Code of Criminal   Procedure.   Further, the  Act also not classify the violation   of the various provisions of the Act   or order  made
thereunder or of any direction given in pursuance of that Act or such order and only provides for punishment   which may extend  to  five years and fine. 
The quantum of punishment for various offences is left to the discretion of the court.  It is proposed  to classify offences committed.   It is also proposed 
that the maximum  punishment under the Foreigners Act may be  upto eight years  and fine upto Rs. 50,000.  The enhancement of punishment will have
the following effects, namely:-
 
(i)
                 serious  offences will become triable by the Court of Sessions; and
 
(ii)        the court will be required to give notice to the State Government thereby affording it an opportunity to oppose the bail application under
proviso to sub-section (l) of section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
 
(iii)       The Bill seeks to achieve the aforesaid  objects.

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorized by the
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present    this Fifty-eighth Report on the Explosive Substances (Amendment) Bill, 1999.
2.         In pursuance of the rule relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in
consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred * the Explosive Substances (Amendment) Bill, 1999 (Annexure-I), as introduced in the
Rajya Sabha on 23 December 1999, and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.         The Bill seeks to amend the relevant provisions of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 by putting more lethal explosives, namely,
RDX, PETN, HMX and other similar explosives or a combination thereof and remote control devices for causing explosion, under ‘Special
Category Explosive Substances’ and to provide for enhancement in maximum punishment for offences committed with such explosive
substances.
4.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill explains that in the recent past there have been incidents of bomb blasts on a very
large scale in some parts of the country particularly in Jammu and Kashmir, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Bihar, West Bengal and the
North-East causing huge loss to life and property. It further explains that terrorists and anti-national elements have, through clandestine means,
acquired research  development explosive (RDX), pentra erythritol tetra nitrate (PETN), high melting explosive (HMX) and other similar types
of explosive substances. These explosives, having high plasticity and low evaporation, are difficult to detect in the normal course. At the same
time, they are far more lethal in their potential for damage than the conventional explosives. Use of such explosives by terrorists and anti-
national elements has not only endangered human life but has also caused a great threat to the security environment of the  country.
4.1       The Statement also explains   that in the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 which provides for the punishment to any person who causes
an explosion likely to endanger life or property, or who attempts to cause such an explosion or makes or has in his possession explosive
substance with intent to endanger life or property, there is no distinction between offences involving use of conventional explosives as
compared with offences committed with more lethal explosives e.g., RDX, PETN, HMX, LTPE and other similar explosives. There is also a
need that explosions caused by use of Remote Control Devices should attract more severe punishment.
5.         The Ministry of Home Affairs  in its Background Note on the  Bill has stated that the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, in its present 
form does not discriminate  between the conventional  type of explosives   and the more  sophisticated type of explosives as are being  used by
the terrorists/militants in carrying out their operations at present.  It has further been stated that it is with a view to checking the rising trend of
violence and terrorism   by extremists and anti-national   elements in various parts of the country by using sophisticated explosives like

5.2       In the backdrop of the situation as explained above, it is proposed to amend the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 by providing for the
sophisticated type of explosives under the definition of  ‘Special Category   Explosive Substances’   and to provide for enhanced punishment
for offences committed with such explosives.
5.3       The salient features of the new legislation as enumerated  in the Background Note  are as follows:-
(i)         A new section (Section 2 (b) ) after the existing Section 2,  provides for classification   of  ‘Special Category Explosive Substances’. 
The proposed amendment is as under:-
 
the expression “special category explosive substance” shall be deemed to include research  development explosive (RDX), penta  
erythritol    tetra nitrate (PETN), high melting explosive  (HMX), tri nitro toluene (TNT), low temperature plastic explosive
(LTPE), composition exploding (CE)(2,4,6 phenyl methyl nit amine or tartly), OCTOL (mixture of high melting explosive and tri
nitro toluene), plastic explosive kirkee-1 (PEK-1) and RDX/TNT compounds and other similar type of explosives  and  a   
combination   thereof   and   remote  control  devices causing explosion.
(ii)        Sections 3,4 and 5 of the existing Act which provide for punishment for the offences committed  with conventional explosives, are also
proposed to be amended by providing for enhanced punishment for offences committed with special category explosives.  The
proposed amendments to these Sections are as under:-

6.         The Committee examined the Bill in its sitting held on  8 February 2000.  The concerned Special Secretary in the Ministry of Home
Affairs made a  presentation on the Bill.   The presentation  revolved round the circumstances as explained in the  preceding paragraphs, which
led the  Government  to come forward  with suitable amendments  to the provisions of the existing  Act. 
6.1       The Special Secretary explained   to the Committee that the production and use of explosive substances was regulated under two Acts,
namely, the Explosives  Act, 1884, and the Explosive   Substances  Act, 1908.  The Department of Industrial   Development   administered the
former, the main objective of which was to regulate the manufacture, possession, use, sale,  transport, import and export of various explosives  
in   the country.  The Ministry of Home Affairs administered   the latter  which    broadly dealt with the punishment to any person who caused
an explosion likely to endanger life    or property or attempted to cause such explosion or made or had in his  possession any explosive  
substance  with an intention   to endanger life or property.  He informed   the Committee   that from the time of militancy  in Punjab, internal
security had become much more complex as sophisticated   weapons, equipment   and explosives  were increasingly being used.  The use of
such weapons and explosives  had not remained confined to Punjab  and Jammu and Kashmir, but it had  also spread to the North-East and 
certain other parts of the country.  He  further stated that the  Pakistan’s  intelligence   agency  ISI was mainly   responsible for that.   Terrorists
trained ,  equipped and indoctrinated  by them had taken  a heavy toll of innocent  lives  in India. 
6.2       He informed the Committee that there had been more than  5,000 explosions  in the last ten to twelve years and the property  destroyed
as a result  of  them   was about Rs.2,000  crore.  The intensity as well as frequency of the explosions had increased manifold in the last four
years.  From 1996 to October 1999, there had been more than 2000 explosions in which 1200 persons lost their lives.  With the advancement in

technology, the explosions that were being caused   by the terrorists were becoming   increasingly   sophisticated, capable   of wreaking
devastation  of a much greater dimension than the conventional explosives.  The explosives being used had high plasticity, low evaporation and
were difficult  to detect.   They were   also easy to carry  and  were  far  more lethal   in nature.    It was, therefore, felt necessary that high-
technology  modern    explosives,   including explosives  which were remote-controlled,  electronically-operated, were put in a special category
for the purpose of punishment that was provided  in the Act.  However, there was need to make a distinction between the types of explosives as
it was not legally tenable   to provide for same kind   of punishment   for   different types of explosives.  He further explained that the Bill
sought  to enhance the punishment not only in the case of special category   explosives but in the case of ordinary explosives as well.  Apart
from this, the punishment had been authorized keeping in view the direction of the Supreme Court.
6.3.      The Special Secretary also informed that the Bill under the consideration of the Committee was the same, which had lapsed due to
dissolution  of Twelfth  Lok Sabha  though  it  was   passed by it on 17  December,1998.
7.         Members raised following points and sought clarifications thereon: 
(a)        While in Clauses 4 and 5, there was provision for ‘rigorous imprisonment’, it was only  ‘imprisonment’ in the case of Clause
3.  It would be proper to explicitly  mention the word ‘rigorous’ in Clause 3 as well.
(b)        The expression ‘explosive substance’ was not fully  descriptive.   If in future, a new type of explosive material was developed
which was outside the purview of the amended Act then what  would be the solution?  There was need to insert or add a clause
or a sentence in the Bill to take care of  the occurrence of such a phenomenon.
(c )       Section 6 of the Act says “Any person who by the supply of or solicitation for money, the providing of premises, the supply  of
materials,  or in any manner whatsoever, procures , counsels, aids, abets, or is accessory to, the commission of any offence
under this Act shall  be  punished with the punishment provided for the offence”.  As  per this clause, if anybody, in  any way,
was accessory to the commission of any offence, he could be punished with death penalty.   Did it mean that a person who did
not have a criminal intention could be punished to the extent of death penalty?
(d)        In Clauses 4 (a) and 4 (b), the words  “an explosion in India” and “injury to property in India” had been used, respectively.  
However, there was no mention of any of these expressions in Section 3.
(e)        If one referred  to Clause 4 (b) of the Bill, an inference may be  drawn  that if a  person  made or had in his possession or under
his control any explosive  substance  which led to an explosion,  he could be punished with rigorous  imprisonment for life or
with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may  extend to only  ten years, whereas in Clause 3, there was a provision for
death penalty if an explosion took place.  Why there was a contradiction between Clauses 3 and 4? In both the cases, explosion
might cause loss to life or property, then why there should be difference in  punishment?
8.         The Special Secretary replied to some of the issues/queries.  The Chair also clarified the position in regard to some of the
issues/queries.       
9.         The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its sitting held on 8 February 2000.
10.       The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 13 March 2000.
11.     The observations/views/suggestions of the Committee with regard to the principal changes proposed in the Bill are given below:
Clause 2
11.1     Clause 2 is the substitution of existing Section 2 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and seeks to add the definition of ‘special
category explosive substances’.  The expression ‘special category explosive substances’ inter alia includes RDX, PETN, HMX, TNT, LTPE,
OCTOL etc. and a combination thereof and remote control devices causing explosion.
11.2     The Committee felt that the definition of the expression ‘special category explosive substances’ was not comprehensive keeping
in view the future technological   developments in this field and wanted to know that if in future some explosive of  a  different type
were to be developed and if the substance did   not  fit into the definition  given  in the  clause  of  the Bill,   the  purpose  of  the 
legislation would be defeated.   Hence, a provision may be added in the clause to include any type of explosive or in the alternative the
Committee suggested that Government may be empowered  to  issue  notification  from  time  to  time  thereby including   any new
type of explosive substance which might be developed in future so as to obviate the necessity  of going through the  legislative process
of frequently amending the law. 
11.3     Subject to this the clause was  adopted.
Clause 3
11.4     Clause 3 of the bill provides for enhanced punishment to any person who unlawfully and maliciously   causes an explosion likely to
endanger life or property.  According to this clause, if any damage to life or property is caused by the explosion of any explosive substance,
the punishment may be for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term  which  may  extend  to  ten  years and shall also be liable
to fine, while if any damage is caused due to explosion of any special category explosive substance, death penalty or imprisonment for life and
fine have been prescribed.
11.5     The Committee pointed out that the phrase ‘imprisonment for life’ in clause 3 had not been qualified by the term ‘rigorous’ as had been
done in clause 4(b)(ii) and clause 5(b) of the Bill .  Although life imprisonment included rigorous imprisonment,   the   Committee  
recommended   that   the term ‘rigorous’ may be added before the phrase ‘imprisonment for life’ wherever it occurred in the Bill for
the sake of uniformity and clarity.   Thereupon,  the    Ministry’s     representative      stated       that        it       would be better   to clarify the
position in the Act itself, even if there were other extant laws  like Section 53-A(4) of   IPC and Section 433-A of Cr.P.C. which clearly
clarified that life imprisonment meant rigorous imprisonment for not less than 14 years.
11.6     It was also pointed out that the proposed amendment did not provide for minimum punishment. The Committee felt that the
provision of minimum punishment might be provided in the clause.
11.7     It was further pointed out that the words ‘an explosion in India’ and ‘injury to property in India’ had been used in clauses 4(a) and 4(b)
respectively, but the reference to  ‘India’ had not been made in clause 3. The Committee recommended that the necessity  of making a

reference to ‘India’ in clause 3  may be examined.
11.8     Subject to this the clause was adopted.
Clause 4
11.9     Clause 4 provides for punishment for attempt to cause explosion or for making or keeping explosive substance with intent to  endanger 
life or  property.  In  the case of  possession of any explosive substance, provision has been made for life imprisonment or imprisonment for a
term which may extend to ten years and shall also include fine, while in the case of possession of any explosive substance of special category a
person may be   awarded   with   rigorous  imprisonment for life or with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to ten years and shall also be
liable to fine.
11.10   A point relating to the aspect of mens rea was raised during the discussion and the Committee wanted to know whether a person in the
absence of criminal intention could be punished to that extent as prescribed under Section 6 of Explosive Substances Act, 1908 read with
clause 3 of the Bill.
11.11   It was also pointed out that under clause 3 if any person was found guilty, he might be punished with imprisonment for life or death,
while in case of a person found guilty under clause 4, punishment was rigorous imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term
which may extend to ten years.  In this context, a view was expressed as to how different punishment had been prescribed for the same
offence. 
11.12   The Committee directed the Ministry to examine the above points from  various angles including the legal angle.
11.13   Subject to this the clause was adopted.
Clause 5
11.14   Clause 5 provides for punishment for making or possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances.   If any person who makes  or 
knowingly has  in possession or under his control any explosive substance or special category explosive substance, under such circumstance
which may give rise to a reasonable suspicion that he is not making it or does not have it in his possession for a lawful object,  he is punishable
for a term which may extend  to ten  years  and  also  liable  to  be  fined  for possessing explosive substances, while rigorous imprisonment for
life or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may   extend   for ten years along with fine is prescribed for possessing special category
explosive substance.
11.15   An apprehension was expressed that the definition of “explosive substance” given under clause 2 had very wide connotations so that
any person suspected to be in possession of any explosive substance under clause 5 might be held guilty under clause 3 of the Bill.  Since
provision of the Bill confer strict liability, the onus would be on the accused and in the absence of adequate safeguards in clause 5, it was
likely to be misused and might cause undue harassment to innocent persons.  The Committee felt that the Government may examine the
feasibility of incorporating suitable safeguards in clause 5 against possible misuse of the power conferred on the executive authority.
11.16   The provisions under clause 5 are ambiguous as to who would exercise power thereunder.  The Committee recommended that
explicit provisions may be incorporated prescribing levels of authority for the exercise of power.
11.17   Subject to this the clause was adopted.  
Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title
12.       Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which were of consequential or drafting nature,
namely, “1999” and “Fiftieth” to be substituted by “2000” and “Fifty-first”, respectively.
General Observations
13.       Section 7 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 provides that no Court shall proceed with the trial of any person for an offence under 
this Act except with the consent of the Central Government.  In this context, the Committee traced the historical background of the enactment
of the law to the Bengal Partition of 1905 and its aftermath.   After some deliberations it was suggested that such kind of    restriction on
the trial of the offence under the Act needed to be reviewed in the contemporary situation. In this context, it was also suggested that
the Government may examine the feasibility of amending Section 7 in such a way so that no Court shall take cognisance of any offence
against the Act except with the consent of the District Magistrate.
13.1     The Committee expressed its serious concern over the undue delay in filing charge-sheet against the person involved in
terrorist/subversive activities and recommended expeditious trial within a given time frame.
13.2     The Committee was of the view that the Government may bring in a comprehensive piece of legislation to deal with all kinds of
terrorist/subversive activities to suit the existing situation.
14.       A communication of interim nature dated 29 February 2000 (Annexure-II) has been received from the Ministry of Home Affairs inter
alia stating   that   it    would  be necessary to consult the Ministries of Law and Defence in respect of the suggestions/observations made in the
Committee on the Bill. It has also been stated that it would be necessary to make a reference to the State Governments for collection of certain
data sought by Members during the discussion on the Bill. As the process of consultation with the Ministries and collection of information
from the State Governments will take quite some time, the Ministry has requested for grant of time (say about two months or so) so that a final
view can be formulated and a complete reply furnished to the Committee.
5.         The Committee directs the Government to examine the specific views/suggestions expressed/made by it during the course of
clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill, before piloting the same in Parliament. The Committee desires that its general observations
on the proposed legislation may also be examined by the Government.

5.        At the beginning of his presentation, the Special Secretary gave a brief outline of the background to the proposed amendment to the
Explosive Substances Act, 1908.  He stated that production and use of explosive substances was regulated   under two  Acts, namely,   the
Explosives  Act, 1884 and the  Explosive   Substances  Act, 1908, which were administered   by Ministries of Industry  and  Home Affairs, 
respectively. The prime objective of the  former Act was to regulate the manufacture, possession, use, sale, transport, import and export  of
various  explosives  in the country.  The latter Act dealt with punishment to any person who caused an explosion or attempted to cause an
explosion or had in his possession any explosive substances with an intention to endanger life or property.
 
5.1       The Special Secretary told the Committee that the use of sophisticated   lethal explosives had become rampant by the
terrorists/militants causing great havoc  in the country during the last twelve to thirteen years,  the intensity of which had gone up
especially during the past three to four years.  He informed the Committee that the terrorist activities had caused more than 5000
explosions in the last ten to twelve   years  and the property destroyed because of those explosions was about Rs.2000 crores.  During
the  years 1996, 97, 98 and upto October, 1999  there  had  been  more than 2000 explosions  in which  1200  persons  had  been
killed.    He stated that these explosives had high plasticity, low evaporation  and were difficult to detect.   These were easy  to carry and far
more lethal in nature which necessitated stringent punishment for persons indulging   in  activities connected with such  explosives  by
differentiating  these explosives  from the conventional  ones.  Hence, high lethal  explosives  of later generation such as research development 
explosive (RDX), penta erythritol tetra nitrate (PETN), high melting explosive (HMX),  tri nitro toluene (TNT), low temperature plastic
explosive  (LTPE), composition exploding (CE)(2,4,6 phenyl methyl nitramine or tetryl), OCTOL (mixture of high melting explosive and tri
nitro toluene), plastic explosive kirkee-1 (PEK-1) and RDX/TNT compounds  including those remote controlled & electronically  operated
were put under ‘Special Category Explosive Substances’ and were  incorporated in clause 2(b) of the Bill.
 
5.2       He further stated that the amendments to clauses 3,4 & 5 of the Explosive   Substances Act, 1908 had been proposed in the Bill in order
to enhance punishment not only in regard to the special category   of explosives  but even in regard to ordinary  category of explosives.  He 
mentioned  that the phrases  like ‘imprisonment for life’  in  place   of  ‘transportation    for   life’, ‘liable   to  fine’    in    place    of   ‘fine may 
be  added’    had   been

included in the Bill to rationalise  punishment.  Further, higher punishment including death  sentence  had  also  been  proposed  in  regard 
to special category explosive substances.   He emphasised   that   the  punishment in the existing Act had been rationalised keeping in view
the direction of  the Supreme Court.
5.3       The Special Secretary also  informed  that the Bill under the consideration   of Committee was the same, which had lapsed due to
dissolution  of Twelfth  Lok Sabha  though  it  was   passed by it on 17  December 1998.
6.         Thereafter, the Chairman and members  raised certain queries  which were replied to by the Special Secretary.
7.         The Committee then took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Explosive Substances (Amendment) Bill, 1999.
Clause 2
7.1.0.   Clause 2  is the substitution of existing Section 2 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and seeks to add the definition   of ‘special
category explosive substances’.  The expression ‘special category explosive  substances’ inter alia includes RDX, PETN, HMX, TNT,
LTPE, OCTOL etc. and a     combination thereof and remote control devices causing explosion.
 
7.1.1    The Committee felt that the definition of the expression ‘special category explosive substances’   was not comprehensive 
keeping  in view the future technological   developments in this field and wanted to know that if in future some explosive of  a 
different type were to be developed and if the substance did not fit into the definition  given  in the  clause  of  the Bill,   the 
purpose  of  the  legislation would be defeated.   Hence, a provision may be added in the clause to include any type of explosive or
in the alternative the Committee suggested that Government may be empowered  to  issue  notification  from  time  to  time 
thereby including   any new type of explosive substance which might be developed in future so as to obviate the necessity  of going
through the  legislative process of frequently amending the law. 
 
7.1.2    Subject to this the clause was  adopted.
Clause 3
7.2       Clause 3 of the Bill provides for enhanced punishment to any person who unlawfully and maliciously   cause an explosion likely to
endanger life or property.  According to this clause, if any damage to life or property is caused by the explosion of any explosive
substance, the punishment may be for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall
also be liable to fine, while if any damage is caused due to explosion of any special category explosive substance, death penalty or
imprisonment for life and fine have been prescribed.
 
7.2.1    The Committee pointed out that the phrase ‘imprisonment for life’ in clause 3 had not been qualified by the term ‘rigorous’ as had
been done in clause 4(b)(ii) and clause 5(b) of the Bill .   It  was   noted   that   although   life   imprisonment included rigorous
imprisonment, the Committee recommended that the term ‘rigorous’ may be added before the phrase ‘imprisonment for life’
wherever it occurred in the Bill for the sake of    uniformity   and   clarity .   Thereupon, the Ministry’s  representative stated that it
would      be    better     to
   clarify  the  position  in  the Act  itself, even if there were other extant laws  like Section    53-A(4) of   IPC and
Section 433-A of Cr.P.C. which clearly clarified that life imprisonment meant rigorous imprisonment for not less than 14 years.
 
7.2.2    It was also pointed out that the proposed amendment did not provide for minimum punishment. The Committee felt that
the provision of minimum punishment might be provided in the clause.

7.2.3    It was further pointed out that the  words ‘an explosion in India’ and ‘injury to property in India’ had been used in clauses 4(a) and
4(b) respectively, but the reference to  ‘India’ had not been made in clause 3. The Committee recommended that the necessity  of
making a reference to ‘India’ in clause 3  may be examined.
 
7.2.4    Subject to this the clause was adopted.
Clause 4
7.3.0    Clause 4 provides punishment for attempt to cause explosion or for making or keeping explosive substance with intent to endanger
life or property.  In the case of  possession of any explosive substance, provision  has  been  made for  life   imprisonment
or imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also  include fine, while in the case of possession of any explosive
substance of special category a person may be awarded with rigorous imprisonment for life or with rigorous imprisonment which may
extend to ten years. 
 
7.3.1    A point relating to aspect of mens rea was raised during the discussion and the Committee wanted to know whether a person in the
absence of criminal intention could be punished to that extent as prescribed under Section 6 of Explosive Substances Act, 1908 read with
clause 3 of the Bill.
 
7.3.2    It was also pointed out that under clause 3 if any person was found guilty, he might be punished with imprisonment for life or
death, while in case of a person found guilty under clause 4, punishment was rigorous imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a
term which may extend to ten years.  In this context, a view was expressed as to how different punishment had been prescribed for the
same offence. 
 
7.3.3    The Committee directed the Ministry to examine the above points from  various angles including the legal angle.
 
7.3.4    Subject to this the clause was adopted.
Clause 5
7.4.0    Clause 5 provides punishment for making or possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances.   If any person who makes  or 
knowingly has  in possession or under his control any explosive substance or special category explosive substance, under such
circumstance which may give rise to a reasonable suspicion that he is not making it or does not have it in his possession for a lawful
object.  In such a situation he is punishable for a term which may extend to ten years and also liable to be fined for possessing explosive
substances, while rigorous imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend for ten years along with fine is
prescribed for possessing special category explosive substance.
 
7.4.1    An apprehension was expressed that the definition of “explosive substance” given under clause 2 had very wide connotations so
that any person suspected to be in possession of any explosive substance under clause 5 might be held guilty under clause 3
of the Bill.  Since provision of  the Bill confer strict liability, the onus would be on the accused and in the absence of adequate safeguards
in clause 5, it was likely to be misused and might cause undue harassment to innocent persons.  The Committee felt that the Government
may examine the feasibility of incorporating suitable safeguards in clause 5 against possible misuse of the power conferred on  the
executive authority.
7.4.2    The provisions under clause 5 are ambiguous as to who would exercise power thereunder.   The Committee recommended that
explicit provisions may be incorporated prescribing levels of authority for the exercise of power.
7.4.3    Subject to this the clause was adopted.  
Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title
8.         Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which were of consequential or drafting
nature, namely, “1999” and “Fiftieth” to be substituted by “2000” and “Fifty-first”, respectively.
 
General observations
8.1       Section 7 of  the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 provides that  no Court shall proceed with the trial of any person for an offence
against this Act except with the consent of the Central Government.  In this context, the Committee traced the historical background of the
enactment of the law,  to the Bengal Partition of 1905 and its aftermath.  After some deliberations it was suggested that such kind of
restriction on the trial of the offence under the Act needed to be reviewed in the contemporary situation. 
 
9.1       The Committee expressed its serious concern over the undue delay in filing charge-sheet against the person involved in
terrorist/subversive activities and recommended expeditious trial within a given time frame.
 
9.2       The Committee was of the view that the Government may bring in a comprehensive piece of legislation to deal with all
kinds of terrorist/subversive activities to suit the existing situation.
 
10.       The Committee then directed the Government to examine the specific views /suggestions expressed/made by it during the
course of clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill, before piloting the same in Parliament. The Committee desired that its general
observations on the proposed legislation may also be examined by the Government

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
In the recent past there have been incidents of bomb blasts on a very large scale in some parts of the country particularly in Jammu and
Kashmir, Tamil Nadu,Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Bihar, West Bengal and the North-East causing huge loss to life and property. Terrorists and
anti-national elements have, through clandestine means, acquired research development explosive (RDX), penta erythritol tetra nitrate (PETN),
high melting explosive (HMX) and other similar types of explosive substances. These explosives, håving high plasticity and low evaporation,
are difficult to detect in the normal course.At the same time, they are far more lethal in their potential for damage than the conventional
explosives. Use of such explosives by terrorists and anti-national elements has not only endangered human life but has also caused a great
threat to the security environment of the country.
 
2.         In the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 which provides for the punishment to any person who causes an explosion likely to endanger
life or property, or who attempts to cause such an explosion or måkes or has in his possession explosive substance with intent to endanger life
or property, there is no distinction between offences involving use of conventional explosives as compared with offences committed with more
lethal explosives, e.g., RDX, PETN, HMX, LTPE and other similar explosives. There is also a need that explosion caused by use of Remote
Control Devices should attract more severe punishment. To overcome these deficiencies, it is proposed to amend the Act by putting more lethal
explosives, viz., RDX, PETN, HMX and other similar explosives or a combination thereof and remote control devices for causing explosion
under 'Special Category Explosive Substances' and to provide for enhancement in maximum punishment for offences committed with such
explosive substances by amending the relevant provisions of the Act.
3.         The Bill seeks to give effect to the above proposed amendments in the Act.

REPORT
 
The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions:
 
            (a)        To deal with all matters relating to internal security;
(b)        To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State relations;
(c )       Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language and the provisions of the
Official Language Act, 1963;
(d)        To discharge certain basic functions like notification of assumption of office by the President and the Vice-
President; notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers; notification of appointment,
resignation and removal of Governors and Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors, Chief Commissioners
and Administrative Officers in Union Territories;
(e)        To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation, census of population, National Anthem, National Flag,
etc.; and
(f)        To deal with all constitutional provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and all other matters
relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding those with which the Ministry of External Affairs is
concerned.
2.         To discharge the above functions, the Ministry has been divided into five Departments:
(i)         Department of Internal Security – to deal with Police, Law and Order and rehabilitation;
(ii)        Department of States – to deal with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations, Union Territories and Freedom
Fighters’ Pension;
(iii)       Department of Official Language – to deal with the implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating
to Official Language and provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963;
(iv)       Department of Home – to deal with notification of assumption of office by the President and Vice-President,
notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers, etc.; and
(v)        Department  of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs – to deal with all constitutional provisions with respect to the State of
Jammu and Kashmir and all other matters relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding those with which
the Ministry of External Affairs is concerned.
3.         On behalf of the Ministry, ten Demands have been presented to Parliament.
4.         In Vol. I of the Demands for Grants, there are five Demands namely, (I) Demand No. 45 – Ministry of Home Affairs; (ii)
Demand No 46 – Cabinet; (iii) Demand No. 47 – Police; (iv) Demand No. 48 – Other Expenditure of the Ministry of Home
Affairs; and (v) Demand No. 49 – Transfers to Union Territory Governments.
5.         Vol. II of the Demands for Grants relates to Union Territories (without Lagislature), namely, Demand No. 99 – Andaman
and Nicobar Islands; Demand No. 100 – Chandigarh; Demand No. 101 – Dadra and Nagar Haveli; Demand No. 102 – Daman and
Diu and Demand No. 103 – Lakshadweep. The entire Budget of the Union Territories  (without Legislature) on the Plan as well as
Non-Plan side is reflected in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs.

12.       Demand Nos. 99, 100, 101, 102 and 103 which are given in Volume-II of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, relate to Union Territories (without Legislature), namely Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra &
Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep, respectively. The entire budget of the Union Territories (without Legislature) on
the Plan as well as Non-Plan side is reflected in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry. Though the budget of these Union
Territories forms part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, being the nodal Ministry, it, however, does not dilute the responsibilities
of the Ministries of the Central Government from scrutinising and sanctioning the schemes under their purview. The factual
position regarding budgetary procedure in this regard is that the entire budget requirement for Plan and Non-Plan, revised
estimates for current year and Non-Plan budget estimates for the ensuing year is discussed by the Ministry of Finance in the pre-
budget meetings with the representatives of the concerned Union Territories and Ministry of Home Affairs. An overall ceiling is
fixed in respect of each Union Territory . Annual Plan allocations for the ensuing year are decided by the Planning Commission.
The Union Territory Administrations, prepare budgetary   break-up showing budget provisions according to their respective
budgetary heads and also showing the allocation against Ministries/Departments of the Central Government administratively
concerned. This budgetary break-up is included in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs.

13.       The Committee began consideration of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in its meeting   held on 23 March 2000. 
The Home Secretary, while making a presentation before the Committee vis-à-vis Demands of the Ministry, stated that the total
budget for the year 2000-2001 was estimated at Rs.13,326.98 crores with a very meagre plan    component of Rs.1,702.29 crores
and a much larger non-plan component of Rs.11,624.69 crores.  The Home Secretary informed the Committee that the largest
chunk of the budget of Ministry of Home Affairs went to the Police at it was the mainstay of the Ministry’s functioning.  The next
largest share was that of the seven Union Territories which were directly administered by the Ministry.
14.       The Home Secretary, while comparing the figures of the last five years’ (1996-2001) budget estimates in respect of each
grant of the Ministry, stated that Grant No.45 – Ministry of Home Affairs registered a quantum jump of Rs.615.50 crores at B.E.
level of 2000-2001 mainly on account of the forthcoming census.  Regarding Grant No.46 – Cabinet, the Ministry had neither any
role nor any control (an amount of  Rs.145 crores has been projected in BE 2000-2001).  In respect of Grant No.47 – Police, the
Home Secretary stated that it pertained to the most substantial functional area of the Ministry as it covered the Central Para
Military Forces and other Central Police Organisations.  He submitted that more funds would be required under that head during
the next five to seven years.  In so far as Demand No.48 – Other   Expenditure of    Ministry  of  Home Affairs was concerned, he
stated that it had stayed nearly at the R.E. level of the outgoing financial year.  Moving on to the Demand No.49 – Transfer to
Union Territories, the Home Secretary stated that Union Territories (with legislatures) were allocated Rs.728.96 crores in B.E.
1999-2000 out of which Rs.483.96 crores were under Plan and Rs.245 crores under Non-Plan.  The allocation was increased to
Rs.828.99 crores with Rs.516.49 crores for Plan and Rs.312.50 crores for Non-Plan at the R.E. stage.  He submitted that Delhi
and Pondicherry might feel starved  in the financial year 2000-2001, especially with regard to their plan allocation which was
pegged at Rs.483.96 crores same as was the B.E. 1999-2000.  As for Union Territories (without legislatures) Grants Nos.99-103,
Rs.2,069.16 crores were allocated in B.E. 1999-2000 with a Plan component of Rs.597.63 crores which was enhanced to
Rs.691.60 crores at R.E. stage.  However, B.E. 2000-2001 for Union Territories (without legislatures) was kept at the level of
B.E. 1999-2000.  The Home Secretary submitted that it happened despite strident demands of the Union Territories for a higher
Plan allocation and Ministry’s unreserved support to their demands.  He urged upon the Committee to consider recommending
higher Plan allocations for Union Territories.
15.       The Home Secretary further elaborated that of the total budget of Ministry of Home Affairs, 53% went into salaries; 17%
into other establishment cost; 9% went into grants-in-aid to State Governments; 3% to arms and ammunitions; 4% to machinery,
equipment and motor vehicles; and 6% to works.  He submitted before the Committee that most of the manpower with the
Ministry of Home Affairs consisted of combatants who needed weapons, mobility, communication equipment and training for the
maximisation of their outputs.  They also needed houses to live in and other infrastructure for their operations.   He felt that those
critical aspects were not adequately addressed in the budget of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  He admitted that it was true that at
times the funds allotted to the Ministry for various provisions, procurements as also for upgradation and acquisition of  new
technologies, could not be utilised.    The reasons for non-utilisation of allocated funds were many including cumbersome official
procedures and regulations.  He stated that a time had come when the Ministry would have to act according to a comprehensive
plan spread over the next five years, to upgrade the men, the materials and the skills comprising Ministry’s forces.  It had become
necessary because the threats to the national security had not only increased spatially and in terms of numerical incidents but also
in terms of focus, intensity, virulence and commitment.   The Home Secretary  further  stated   that  the  proportion of mercenaries
and foreigners among the militants, who were equipped with state–of-the-art weaponry and technology,   had increased
substantially during the last couple of years and as a result the complexion of militancy and terrorism in the country had
undergone a drastic change.   The answer to those developments lied in constantly upgrading the equipment and skills available  
with    the   forces   so that they were able to keep a step ahead of their adversaries.  He
conceded that at the moment forces did not possess that supremacy over the militants.   It was primarily due to this that the
militants were able to strike at will at the security forces as well as the soft targets.   He informed the Committee that the Ministry
was working on plans to strengthen and modernise security forces, and very soon  proposals would be brought for Government’s
decision to raise new battalions.  He further informed that as per the initial estimates, 261 new battalions would be required to be
raised to meet the demands of border security and internal security.   He also informed that as per the decision of the Cabinet
Committee on Security, an inter-ministerial Group had been set up to examine the futuristic assessment made by the Ministry. 
Elucidating the financial implications of the futuristic assessment, the Home Secretary stated that an effort had been made to cut
down costs by proposing restructuring of the existing battalions.   The augmentation plan would require Rs.2083 crores as non-
recurring expenditure, Rs.2730 crores as capital cost and Rs.1600 crores as annual recurring cost.  The funds needed to back up
the futuristic assessment would be required over the next five years.  The Home Secretary urged upon the Committee to support
the augmentation plan to strengthen Ministry’s hands.
16.       Thereafter, the Home Secretary informed that BSF, CRPF, ITBP, CISF, NSG and Assam Rifles had since prepared their
modernisation plans for implementation over a period of five  years and were being processed by the Ministry.  The financial
implication of the plan was to the tune of Rs.4025 crores which included Rs.2530 crores for BSF, Rs.546 crores for CRPF and
Rs.218 crores for ITBP, Rs.101 crores for CISF, Rs.84 crores for NSG and Rs.546 crores for Assam Rifles.  The proposals to
strengthen BSF’s Air Wing and Water Wing by acquiring new aircrafts and watercrafts had been accepted in principle and were

plans of the central forces.
17.       Thereafter, the Home Secretary made a brief mention of the important activities of the Ministry during the outgoing year
and also the initiatives reserved for the next financial year.
18.       With regard to the situation prevailing in Jammu and Kashmir, the Home Secretary stated that the modifications in the
Action Plan, chalked out to tackle militancy, had been implemented on ground.  A sum of Rs.272.57 crores had so far been
released to the Government of Jammu & Kashmir on account of security related expenditure.   Rs.25 crores had been given as

supply of arms and ammunitions to the Jammu & Kashmir Police and Rs.2.39 crores had been released to various automobile
companies for the supply of vehicles to Jammu & Kashmir Police.   A sum of Rs.2.25 crores had been given for civic action
programme.  In addition to that, an amount of Rs.100 crores had been released during the outgoing financial year under the Debt

SITUATION IN JAMMU & KASHMIR
28.       The State of Jammu and Kashmir has been reeling under terrorism for over a decade.   Though our security forces have
persistently been making efforts to stamp out militancy from the troubled State, the aid in the form of men and material, being
extended to the misguided youth of the State from across the border has not allowed the spirits of militants to die.  At a time,
when our forces were beginning to gain a perceptible upper hand over the militants, there came a solid boost from across the
border in the form of large scale infiltration in Kargil.  Post-Kargil phase of militancy in the State has been marked by a subtle
upswing in the violent activities of the militants.  There have been numerous attacks on security forces and establishments located
in the State.  While on the one hand, attacks have been masterminded and targeted at the security forces, on the other, several soft
targets have, very meticulously, been identified such as the Sikh community of the State.   The brutal massacre of  thirty-five  
innocent persons belonging to the Sikh community in the Chatti Singhpura village of Anantnag District of Jammu & Kashmir, has
not only  outraged the entire nation but has also evoked worldwide condemnation. The Chairman of the Committee raised this
issue in the beginning of the meeting of the Committee held on 23 March 2000.  He stated that as per newspaper reports, thirty-
five members of the Sikh community were butchered by heavily-armed gunmen  dressed in military-style fatigues who raided this
typical Kashmiri roadside village along the Anantnag-Pahalgam Highway.  This incident which was the latest in the long series of

killings of innocent persons by militants had stirred the nation’s conscience. The electronic media while covering the tragic
killings showed on Tuesday, 21 March  2000 clippings of relatives of the slain persons who  were highly agitated with anguish
writ large on their faces over the fact that although the news of the killings was sent to the D.C. within half  an hour of the
massacre, he had not cared to visit the spot even after a lapse of about 15 hours (i.e. upto the  time the footage was shot).  The
brief footage undoubtedly conveyed a surcharged atmosphere with kins of the deceased wailing and complaining.   If the episode
of the D.C. was true, then it was a very serious matter and the Committee would like to be fully apprised of the facts in that
behalf.  From newspaper reports it was seen that the militants numbered about thirty-five   to forty  and  were dressed in military
outfits.  In this connection, the Home Secretary should specifically apprise the Committee the kind of intelligence network that
operated in that area. The Committee was quite surprised to note that such a large number of people in uniform in vehicles could
enter the village and commit such heinous crime.   As it was known, army vehicles carried separate type of number plates. 
Therefore, it was very easy to distinguish such vehicles from the ordinary vehicles bearing   transport department number  plates.  
The Committee felt that perhaps it  would not be wrong in concluding that there was an utter failure of intelligence in this case. 
The Chairman  requested the Home Secretary to brief the Committee in detail about the facts and the Government of India’s
reaction thereto and what kind of compensation was  proposed to be given to the next of kin of the bereaved families.
29.       The Committee was informed that during the night intervening March 20-21, 2000, at about 2200 hours, the militants
wearing Army camouflage uniform asked the residents of Chatti  Singhpura Village to assemble for an army operation and
segregated the males from the rest before opening fire.  As a result of  firing, thirty-five Sikhs  were shot dead and one injured.  
The militants also set on fire the middle school building in the village while retreating. However, the issue of intelligence failure
leading to the occurrence of this incident did not get any mention in the  replies of the  Home Secretary and the written responses
of the  Ministry  the points/issues  raised in the meeting.
30.       The Committee has been deeply anguished at the brutal killings of innocent people of Chatti Singhpura Village of
Anantnag District of Jammu & Kashmir and is very much concerned   at    the    rising   number of attacks by the
militants on security forces and their
establishments.  The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to have a comprehensive review of the strategy being
used to fight  the militants.  The situation, grave  as it is, calls for the adoption of a multi-pronged strategy.  The strategy
should not only focus on identifying potential ‘soft targets’ for militants but it should also ensure that our security forces
and establishments do not fall prey to the militants.  The Committee urges upon the Government to spare no stone
unturned to see that the back of the militancy is permanently broken, the nefarious   designs of the hostile neighbouring
country are defeated and normalcy in the beleaguered State is restored.
31.       This gruesome incident was followed by an attack on a BSF camp at Chandpur in Srinagar by a suicide squad of
the militants.  The attack on BSF camp is not an isolated incident rather just one of the series of such incidents.  Evidently,
there has been a calculated spurt in the attacks on security forces.  This needs to be curbed.There is a need for upgrading
security in and around the camps/company headquarters of security  forces.  Adequate  steps should be taken to maintain
foolproof security at all such places in order to see that security forces suffer lesser casualties while engaging the militants.

49.2     ‘Police’ and “Public Order’ being  State subjects as enumerated in List-II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of

responsibility of State Governments to do their level best to generate the maximum possible funds for the modernisation

adversaries  who are equipped with AK-47s and other sophisticated weapon systems.  With the development of 5.56 mm INSAS
by Ordnance Factory Board, more and more such rifles are being inducted in our forces.  This weapon system  is said to be a high
calibrs multi-function system which could prove to be the mainstay of our forces.  At the same time, it is also worthwhile to
mention that the field experience of our Jawans shows that the weapons of AK series  can only    be matched  by none other than
the weapons of AK series itself.  Militants/insurgents often manage to gain an upper hand over  our forces, despite being small in
number, by virtue of being in possession of AK-47s  and 56s.  The Committee was given to understand  that though the weapons
of AK series were being imported albeit in limited  number.  Accordingly, their availability too was limited in some cases being

hour is to prepare a comprehensive and futuristic perspective plan based on scientific assessment of the overall traffic
scenario.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that Delhi Police should prepare a detailed perspective plan which 
takes care of  both present as well as future traffic management   requirements of Delhi.
